newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Copper prices weaken, at six-month lows.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Copper prices weaken, at six-month lows.

text.p: The price of cash copper moved into a contango for the first time in almost a year on Friday, suggesting that a period of tight supply of the flagship industrial metal may be over.
Cash copper had been commanding a premium that had ranged as high as $330 per tonne over three months delivery on the London Metal Exchange.

That backwardation narrowed this week, and Friday saw a sliding market edge into contango when a forward price of less than $2,225 a tonne -- the weakest for six months -- stood just above that for cash metal.
Traders attributed the slide to a rise in global stocks, partly reflecting slow summer conditions, but also to the wider supply/demand balance tilting into surplus.
LME warehouse stocks rose 4,575 tonnes on Friday, taking the total increase for the week to 12,175 tonnes. So far this year stocks have risen by 145,200 tonnes.
Some analysts, however, said stocks were recovering from a low base and the price could be kicked up again by any hiccup in supply.
"The market is moving into surplus but stocks are still very low," said Martin Squires at brokerage Rudolf Wolff.
Another Wolff expert, William Adams, told a conference in Australia this week that the El Nino weather phenomenon had the potential to disrupt metal supply.
Adams said the biggest impact would be on copper, either through heavy rains in South America or drought in Australia.

The effect of weather on copper had been seen earlier in the year when lack of rain lowered water levels in the Fly River in Papua New Guinea, disrupting supplies from The Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd's Ok Tedi mine, he said.

Up to 60 percent of world copper output had the potential to be disrupted by El Nino, a weather condition caused by warming of water in the western Pacific Ocean which creates drought in some areas and heavier-than-normal rainfall in others.
As copper sagged, the price of aluminium remained firm on Friday. Speculators have been scrambling to cover metal for delivery due next week as premiums for nearby supply widened sharply.
Commodity markets generally were quiet and rangebound with no sign of any immediate reaction to new jitters on Wall Street stocks. Much of Europe was closed for the Assumption Day holiday.
Profit-taking plus faltering U.S. gasoline demand and resumed crude oil exports from Iraq weighed on petroleum prices.
